anchorData: SPEED OF SOUND IN AIR: v = 340 m/s everywhere in this unit (about 20 degrees C). Light in air: 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Echo formula: d = vt/2, so t = 2d/v. Minimum distinct echo: the ear separates two sounds only if they are at least 0.1 s apart, so 0.1 s x 340 m/s / 2 = 17 m minimum distance to a reflector. ECHO TABLE (all t values use t = 2d/340): (A) Hell's Gate cliff face, learners stand 85 m away, round trip 170 m, delay 0.50 s, clear distinct echo. (B) Ngong Hills valley wall, 170 m away, round trip 340 m, delay 1.00 s, clear distinct echo. (C) Kisumu school hall, speaker stands 12 m from the far wall, round trip 24 m, delay 0.07 s (less than 0.1 s) so the echo merges with the original voice, and the hall's hard walls and roof keep reflecting so the sound lingers about 1.2 s (reverberation): loud, muddy, drawn out. (D) Nairobi school open grounds: grass field, nearest large hard wall (a classroom block) is 300 m away, round trip 600 m, delay 1.76 s, but the sound has spread out over a huge area and the grass and bushes absorb and scatter it, so the returning sound is too faint to hear: no echo. FIELD ACTIVITY (Lesson 4): learners stand 50 m from the school's long stone wall and clap in time with the returning echo; 10 clap-echo intervals take 2.94 s, so one interval is 0.294 s and d = 340 x 0.294 / 2 = 49.98 m, about 50 m. SURFACE TABLE (approximate share of sound energy reflected): cliff rock 90%, painted concrete wall 85%, wooden board 60%, curtains/cloth 15%, thick grass/foam mattress 10%. LIGHT AND REFLECTION: plane mirror, angle of incidence 40 degrees gives angle of reflection 40 degrees (both measured from the normal). REFRACTION: refractive index n: air 1.00, water 1.33, glass 1.50. Light in water travels at 3.0 x 10^8 / 1.33 = 2.26 x 10^8 m/s; in glass 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. Snell's law n1 sin i = n2 sin r. Ray in air at i = 45 degrees (sin 45 = 0.707): into water sin r = 0.707/1.33 = 0.532, r = 32 degrees; into glass sin r = 0.707/1.50 = 0.471, r = 28 degrees. Apparent depth: Lake Victoria shallow pool with real depth 1.33 m looks 1.33/1.33 = 1.00 m deep. Sound speed in water about 1500 m/s (faster than air 340 m/s). DIFFRACTION: a 340 Hz sound has wavelength 340/340 = 1.0 m; a 1000 Hz sound has wavelength 0.34 m; visible light (green) about 5.5 x 10^-7 m. A classroom doorway is 1.0 m wide. Sound wavelength is comparable to the gap so it spreads strongly; light wavelength is tiny compared to the gap so it barely bends. INTERFERENCE: two speakers each playing 340 Hz (wavelength 1.0 m). Path difference 1.0 m (one whole wavelength) gives constructive interference (loud); path difference 0.5 m (half a wavelength) gives destructive interference (quiet). STATIONARY WAVES: wave relation v = f x wavelength. Nyatiti string 0.60 m long with wave speed 120 m/s on it: fundamental has wavelength 2L = 1.20 m, f = 120/1.20 = 100 Hz; second harmonic 200 Hz (3 nodes including the ends, 2 antinodes). Flute modelled as an open tube 0.34 m long: fundamental wavelength 2L = 0.68 m, f = 340/0.68 = 500 Hz. DOPPLER: ambulance siren emits 700 Hz and moves at 20 m/s along Waiyaki Way; approaching observer hears 700 x 340/(340-20) = 744 Hz; after it passes (receding) observer hears 700 x 340/(340+20) = 661 Hz. So approaching is higher than 700 Hz and receding is lower than 700 Hz. COMMUNICATION: FM radio station carrier frequency 91.0 MHz, radio waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, wavelength = 3.0 x 10^8 / 91.0 x 10^6 = 3.30 m; in FM the sound signal changes the frequency of the carrier, not its amplitude. MEDICINE: ultrasound probe 3.5 MHz; speed of sound in soft tissue 1540 m/s; wavelength = 1540/3.5 x 10^6 = 0.00044 m (0.44 mm); an organ boundary 7.7 cm (0.077 m) deep returns an echo after t = 2 x 0.077/1540 = 1.0 x 10^-4 s (100 microseconds). NOISE (decibels, dB): whisper 30 dB, quiet classroom 50 dB, ordinary conversation 60 dB, Kisumu hall during assembly 85 dB, matatu with loud music 95 dB, safe limit used in class 85 dB for up to 8 hours; exposure above this risks hearing damage.
characters: Grade 10 learners from a Nairobi-area school on a trip: Wanjiru (curious, asks why the voice comes back), Otieno (from Kisumu, notices the hall echo is muddy), Kiprono (from Kericho, measures the delay with a stopwatch), Amina (from Mombasa, draws the models). Teacher: Mr. Mwangi, who guides the trip and the class. Places: Hell's Gate National Park in the Rift Valley (cliff 85 m away, clear 0.50 s echo); Ngong Hills valley (clear echo 1.00 s); school hall in Kisumu (12 m to far wall, muddy loud drawn-out sound); open grounds of a Nairobi school (no echo). Objects: stopwatch, tape measure, plane mirror, ripple tank or PhET simulations, nyatiti (Luo 8-string lyre) with 0.60 m vibrating length, flute, matatu, ambulance on Waiyaki Way, FM radio, ultrasound scanner at a county hospital. Every lesson may rely on: the learners are the same four people, the four echo sites in anchorData, and the Driving Question Board (DQB) and class model that grow lesson by lesson.
outcome: Sound is a mechanical wave that travels from the shouting learner, hits a large hard smooth surface and reflects, obeying the law of reflection, then returns to the ear after a delay equal to 2d/v. At Hell's Gate (0.50 s) and Ngong Hills (1.00 s) the surface is far enough away (more than 17 m) and hard enough that a strong separate echo is heard. In the Kisumu hall the wall is only 12 m away (delay 0.07 s) with many hard surfaces, so reflections overlap the original voice and give a loud, muddy, drawn-out sound (reverberation). On the open Nairobi grounds the sound spreads out, is absorbed by soft grass and the only big wall is 300 m away, so the returned sound is too weak to hear. Other wave behaviours (refraction, diffraction, interference, resonance, Doppler) are explained with the same wave ideas.
conventions: Speed of sound in air is always 340 m/s. Use d = vt/2 and call it the echo-distance formula (t is the total time from sound leaving to sound returning, d is one-way distance). Write the wave equation as v = f x wavelength (wavelength symbol lambda, units m; frequency f in hertz, Hz; speed v in m/s). Time in seconds (s). Echo means a distinct reflected sound heard at least 0.1 s after the original (reflector at least 17 m away); reverberation means overlapping reflections that merge and prolong the sound. Reflection angles are always measured from the normal, not from the surface. Angle of incidence is i, angle of reflection is r (in reflection) and angle of refraction is r in Snell's law. Refractive index n has no units; Snell's law is n1 sin i = n2 sin r. Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave needing a medium; light is a transverse electromagnetic wave that does not need a medium. Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). Strong echo means high percentage of sound energy reflected; weak echo means most is absorbed or scattered. Nodes are points of zero amplitude and antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Pitch depends on frequency; loudness depends on amplitude. Noise levels in decibels (dB). Use Kenyan examples and the 340 m/s figures exactly as in anchorData; do not introduce other numbers for the four echo sites.

lessonMap.focus: Anchoring phenomenon: Echoes at Hell's Gate, Ngong, Kisumu and Nairobi
lessonMap.teaches: Echoes are sound coming back after meeting a surface; observing and describing the four sites and making first predictions and a first echo model
lessonMap.buildsOn: None; launches the phenomenon and uses learners' everyday experience of shouting at walls
lessonMap.usesData: Echo table sites A to D (distances, delays and descriptions of what is heard); no calculations yet beyond noticing the delay

lessonMap.focus: Rectilinear propagation of light and waves
lessonMap.teaches: Light travels in straight lines (shadows, pinhole camera, PhET Geometric Optics); waves are described by rays and the ray model for travelling energy
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 1: the idea that something travels from source to wall and back needs a path
lessonMap.usesData: Light speed 3.0 x 10^8 m/s versus sound 340 m/s; sound path to the cliff in site A drawn as a straight ray

lessonMap.focus: Reflection of waves and the laws of reflection
lessonMap.teaches: Laws of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, and incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 2: ray diagrams and straight-line paths
lessonMap.usesData: Plane mirror example i = 40 degrees gives r = 40 degrees; ripple reflection from a barrier; sound ray hitting the Hell's Gate cliff

lessonMap.focus: Reflection of sound: echo measurement and surfaces
lessonMap.teaches: Calculating echo distance with d = vt/2, the 0.1 s (17 m) condition for a distinct echo, and how hard versus soft surfaces give strong or weak echoes
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 1 and 3: the four sites and the idea that sound reflects following the law of reflection
lessonMap.usesData: Echo table A to D with all delays; field measurement (10 intervals in 2.94 s, 50 m); surface table (90%, 85%, 60%, 15%, 10%)

lessonMap.teaches: Waves change direction when their speed changes on entering a new medium (bent straw, apparent depth, water waves moving from deep to shallow)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 and 4: reflection is wave bouncing back; now the wave goes into the second medium; sound speed differs by medium
lessonMap.usesData: Light speeds in air, water (2.26 x 10^8 m/s) and glass; sound in air 340 m/s versus water 1500 m/s; apparent depth 1.33 m looking like 1.00 m

lessonMap.focus: Snell's law, refractive index and lenses
lessonMap.teaches: Calculating refraction with n1 sin i = n2 sin r and drawing ray diagrams for converging and diverging lenses with uses in spectacles, cameras and microscopes
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lesson 5: speed change causes bending; Lesson 3: normal and angle measurement
lessonMap.usesData: n values 1.00, 1.33 and 1.50; i = 45 degrees gives r = 32 degrees in water and 28 degrees in glass

lessonMap.teaches: Waves spread around edges and through gaps, with most spreading when the gap is comparable to the wavelength, so sound turns corners more than light
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 2 and 4: light seems to go straight and sound is heard around the hall or building; wavelength from v = f x wavelength
lessonMap.usesData: Wavelengths 1.0 m (340 Hz), 0.34 m (1000 Hz) and 5.5 x 10^-7 m (light); 1.0 m doorway

lessonMap.teaches: Superposition: waves meeting add to give constructive interference (path difference of whole wavelengths) or destructive interference (half wavelengths); noise-cancelling headphones
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 4 and 7: reflected sound and diffracted waves overlap and meet; wavelength 1.0 m
lessonMap.usesData: Two speakers at 340 Hz, path difference 1.0 m (loud) and 0.5 m (quiet); the muddy overlapping reflections in the Kisumu hall (site C)

lessonMap.teaches: Stationary waves form when a wave and its reflection interfere in a string or air column, producing nodes and antinodes and set frequencies f = v/2L (resonance and pitch)
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 3 and 8: reflection at ends and interference of the two waves
lessonMap.usesData: Nyatiti 0.60 m string, 120 m/s, 100 Hz and 200 Hz; flute 0.34 m open tube, 500 Hz

lessonMap.teaches: Relative motion of source and observer changes the observed frequency (higher when approaching, lower when receding), with uses in radar and astronomy
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 7 to 9: frequency and wavelength linked by v = f x wavelength and pitch
lessonMap.usesData: Ambulance siren 700 Hz at 20 m/s, 744 Hz approaching and 661 Hz receding

lessonMap.teaches: Applications: FM radio carries sound by changing carrier frequency of radio waves, and ultrasound imaging uses reflected pulses and echo timing to locate tissue boundaries
lessonMap.buildsOn: Lessons 4 and 10: echo timing d = vt/2 and frequency; lessons 2 and 5 for electromagnetic waves
lessonMap.usesData: FM station 91.0 MHz with wavelength 3.30 m; ultrasound 3.5 MHz, 1540 m/s, 7.7 cm depth gives 100 microseconds

lessonMap.focus: Noise pollution and the final model
lessonMap.teaches: Noise sources, health effects and noise-reduction design (absorbing materials, barriers), then the final complete explanation of echoes using all wave behaviours; final DQB review
lessonMap.buildsOn: All lessons 1 to 11: especially 4 (echo distance and surfaces), 8 (interference), 9 (resonance) and 3 (reflection)
lessonMap.usesData: Decibel values (30, 50, 60, 85, 95 dB; 85 dB safe limit); all four echo sites A to D and the surface table to explain the outcome and propose absorbing treatment for the Kisumu hall
